how.head.title: How targum reads Hebrew
how.head.description: The hard parts of Hebrew for a machine, and each one solved on a real text.
how.page.title: How targum reads Hebrew
how.page.lede: Hebrew is easy to read once you know it, and hard for a machine that does not. These are the hard parts, each solved on a real text. Every example is targum's own output, copied from a reader.
how.vowels.title: Hebrew hides its vowels
how.vowels.said: Hebrew is printed without its vowels, and a learner reads by them. targum points every word of a text that came without them, and the reader can take the points off again.
how.spelling.title: One spelling can be five words
how.spelling.said: Without vowels, ספר can be a book, a barber, a border, he counted or he told. Only the sentence says which. targum reads each word in its sentence and files it as the word it is there.
how.kind.name: name
how.prefixes.title: Words wear their prefixes
how.prefixes.said: And, the, in, to, from, that and as are single letters, written onto the front of the next word, often several at once. targum takes them off and files what is left under its dictionary form.
how.roots.title: Roots and patterns
how.roots.said: Most Hebrew words grow from a root of three letters set into a pattern. targum names a verb's root and its pattern, and one word list runs from Genesis to this week's news.
how.speech.title: Speech has no punctuation
how.speech.said: A transcript of speech comes back as one run of words, with no full stop and no comma. targum gives it its sentences back without changing a word that was heard, and times every word to the recording, so the line you read is the line you hear.
how.media.title: Any medium, the right reader
how.media.said: A text is read in the shape it came in. A reel stays upright with its words beside it, a post keeps its author at the top, and a chat stays a chat, each line under the name of whoever sent it.
how.media.chat-from: A building's group chat, read from a screenshot
how.aramaic.title: Aramaic beside the Torah
how.aramaic.said: Onkelos, the Aramaic translation read beside the Torah each week, is a language of its own, and targum keeps a word list of its own for it. A word of Onkelos is filed under its Aramaic headword, apart from the Hebrew it translates.
